newsitem.title: CHINA: China to axe 300 newspapers in one year.
newsitem.headline: China to axe 300 newspapers in one year.

text.p: China's propaganda tsars will axe 300 newspapers in one year as part of a shake-up of an industry seen as tainted by corruption and ideas out of line with Communist Party ideology.

"The State Press and Publications Administration has decided to engage in a drastic shake-up of the newspaper industry and put it in order," the official Ningxia Daily said in an edition seen in Beijing on Thursday.
"(It) will use one year to axe 300 kinds of publicly circulated newspapers," said the newspaper, mouthpiece of the leadership of the northern province of Ningxia.
It did not identify the newspapers that would be shut or say when the crackdown would begin.
The administration planned to merge a number of newspapers of similar nature, such as legal dailies, it said.
China had more than 2,000 government-approved newspapers by the end of 1996, or 10 times the figure before the country opened up to the outside world almost two decades ago, it said.

About one-tenth of the newspapers face a plethora of problems, including small circulation, low quality and the widespread practice of "paid news", or demanding money or gifts in return for positive reports, the Ningxia Daily said.

Some corrupt journalists extort money from local officials and state-owned enterprises by threatening to write negative stories in classified documents read by party leaders. Ambitious officials and enterprises that badly need loans willingly pay bribes.
Communist Party chief and state president Jiang Zemin has declared war on corruption, warning that it could topple the party.

China's propaganda mandarins have launched an authoritarian campaign to stamp out ideas that differ from party precepts, and which has been billed as a crusade to "build spiritual civilisation" -- communist jargon for civic responsibility and social ethics.
In January, China issued directives on how to write news, ordering journalists not to advocate sex, violence and superstition and to fill their news reports with patriotism and socialism.
The communists have maintained an iron grip on the media since coming to power in 1949, viewing it as a tool that must serve party interests.

Last September, Cui Enqing was sacked as president of the Beijing Youth Daily after the Chinese capital's most outspoken newspaper reported a poisoning case that caused a plunge in sales of a state-owned beverage manufacturer.
The ideological axe has also fallen on magazines, books and films.
